title: 32 Effects of late gestational melatonin supplementation on behavior and growth characteristics in Angus beef cows and calves
content:
Abstract
Late gestation is characterized by rapid and substantial fetal growth, which causes heightened metabolic demand on dams. This increased metabolic demand results in a favorable environment for oxidative stress, which can negatively impact dam and offspring health. Melatonin is a versatile hormone with potent antioxidant properties and functions as a neuromodulator, altering oxidative stress and behavioral responses. Our study aims to assess the impact of late gestational melatonin supplementation in Angus beef cows on dam behavior and the programming effects on offspring growth. Pregnant Angus beef cows (n=24) in the third trimester were trained to acquire feed from a Calan gate electronic feeding system and randomly assigned to either the control group (CON) or melatonin group (MEL). Melatonin was dissolved in ethanol and top-dressed on supplemental feed at a dose of 200 µg/kg of body weight. Melatonin supplementation was adjusted weekly based on maternal body weights. Control dams received an equivalent dose of ethanol top dressed on supplemental feed. Treatments started at approximately day 209 of gestation and continued for 54 days. Chute scores, exit velocity score, and exit velocity (m/s) were taken on days 14, 28, and 42 of treatment. Maternal aggression score (MA) and mothering aptitude score (MOM) were collected at birth. Calf morphometrics, including body weight, heart girth, abdominal girth, hip height, curved-crown rump length (CCR), and ponderal index (BW [kg]/CCR [m]3), were collected at birth, 30 and 60 days of age. Chute score, exit velocity, and calf morphometrics were analyzed using GLIMMIX or mixed procedures in SAS, incorporating treatment, time, interactions, and baseline or birth measurements as covariates. MA and MOM scores were evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test.. In dams, no differences (P >0.05) were observed in chute score and exit velocity score between treatments. There was no difference in exit velocity (m/s) of dams between treatments; however, time was significantly different (P< 0.0001) as gestation proceeded. No differences (P >0.05) were found in MA and MOM scores between treatment groups. In calves, there was a tendency for treatment (P=0.08) in body weights, with CON calves being heavier than MEL calves. No differences in treatment were seen for heart girth, abdominal girth, hip height, CCR, and ponderal index. However, time was significant for hip height, CCR, and ponderal index (P< 0.05), indicating growth changes over time regardless of treatment. These results indicate that the dose and timing of melatonin supplementation did not significantly alter physical behaviors in dams. However, further research is needed to evaluate its effects on neurotransmitter production and metabolism in dams and calves and its potential long-term impacts on calf performance.
